title: Sequence-encoded hexagonal lattices in multichannel peptide nanofibrils.
data_url: https://www.rcsb.org/structure/9H7U (atomic model); https://www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb/EMD-51914 (cryo-EM map); EMPIAR-13663 / EMPIAR-13687 (raw cryo-EM movies)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded PDB 9H7U (389 KB mmCIF, 3,888 ATOM lines, 54 chains, all the same 9-residue peptide KVKVSQINM) and confirmed PDB 28XH and 28XG return HTTP 200; PDB 28YD returns 404 (not yet released). Fetched the EMDB entry EMD-51914 metadata (live JSON). Scanned the whole open-access full text (120 KB) and counted every distinct peptide sequence mentioned.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Which peptides formed a hexagonal lattice and which did not (described only in figure captions and running text, never in a table I could download); the existence and size of the EMPIAR-13663 / EMPIAR-13687 raw movie depositions (the European Bioinformatics Institute EMPIAR application programming interface returned 404 for both the bare and prefixed entry URLs); the content of Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 1-3, which the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint timed out on.

a1_downloadable.note: Partly. The deposited structures genuinely download without login (I pulled 9H7U.cif myself). But the data availability statement says further supporting data and all custom analysis scripts are 'available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request', and a patent (EP26197462.0) covers the sequences.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. There is no table anywhere with one row per peptide and an outcome column. The thing a model would predict - does this 9-residue peptide build a hexagonal honeycomb lattice? - exists only as prose and figure captions (for example 'P7 and P8 produce non-striped fibrils'). I would have to hand-build the label by reading the paper.

a3_inputs_present.note: The peptide sequences themselves are written out in the text (KVKVSQINM, RVKVSQINM, KVRVSQINM, GVKVSQINM, YVKVSQINM, KLKLSQINM, KVKVKVSQINM and others), so no accession lookups would be needed - but they too must be transcribed by hand.

a4_units_stated.note: Not really applicable: the main readout is a yes/no morphology call from cryo-electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy. Physical quantities that are given (about 5 nm pore diameter, map resolutions) do carry units in the text.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, decisively. Thirteen peptides in total: DILT1-DILT5 (five lattice formers) plus P1-P8 (eight designed perturbations). The checklist floor is about 400 rows for a classification task. Thirteen is roughly thirty times too few.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1.5 MB of mmCIF atomic models; cryo-EM maps a few hundred MB each
a6_fits_laptop.note: The atomic models are trivially small (9H7U is 389 KB). The EMPIAR raw movie depositions are terabyte-scale and are excluded by the project's own no-raw-data rule, but nothing in the proposed task needs them.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: 9H7U contains exactly the 9-residue KVKVSQINM sequence the paper names for DILT1, in 54 chains, consistent with a multi-hexagon lattice cross-section. Three of the four promised PDB entries are released; 28YD (DILT2 2-2-2) is not yet public.

a8_label_provenance.note: The lattice/no-lattice call comes from real cryo-electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy images, not from another model's output - so provenance is clean in principle. One caveat: some supporting evidence is 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation, which would be a simulated label if mixed in.

existing_models.name: AggBERT (a protein language model, ProtBERT, fine-tuned semi-supervised to predict whether a six-residue peptide forms amyloid fibrils)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported by its authors as state-of-the-art for hexapeptide amyloid prediction, beating simple heuristics and structure-based methods; the exact split was not visible in the search result I retrieved.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I only saw the abstract-level summary, not the discussion.

existing_models.name: Cross-Beta DB predictor (an Extra Trees classifier trained on a curated database of experimentally confirmed cross-beta amyloids)
existing_models.score_and_split: Authors report F1 score 0.852, the highest among the amyloid predictors they compared; split details not retrieved.

existing_models.name: Transformer aggregation-propensity predictors (deep models trained on coarse-grained molecular dynamics aggregation-propensity scores for pentapeptides through decapeptides)
existing_models.score_and_split: One reported about 6% error on aggregation propensity; a hybrid sequence-plus-physicochemical model reported 81.9% accuracy and F1 0.865. Training sets of 62,000+ simulated peptides are described.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model with small CPU-runnable checkpoints)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would be ample for 13 nine-residue peptides - which is exactly the problem: 13 embeddings cannot train or evaluate any head.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the peptide sequences themselves are covered by patent application EP26197462.0 filed by the Max-Planck-Gesellschaft.

integration.partner_dataset: Cross-Beta DB and the amyloid-hexapeptide sets behind AggBERT, plus the Protein Data Bank's amyloid-fibril structures
integration.join_key: peptide sequence string (no standard accession exists for a designed 9-mer)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do the sequence features that predict ordinary cross-beta amyloid formation also predict the much rarer hexagonal, nanochannel-forming lattice - i.e. is 'makes a honeycomb' a special case of 'makes a fibril' or a different rule? The question is good, but with 13 labelled peptides on this side of the join it cannot be answered.

controls.positive_control: DILT1 (KVKVSQINM), whose honeycomb lattice is solved at atomic resolution in PDB 9H7U, must be called a lattice-former by any working model.
controls.negative_control: P7 and P8, the trimeric-junction perturbations that the paper reports give non-striped fibrils - a model must call these negative.
controls.external_validation: Cross-Beta DB and the published hexapeptide amyloid sets provide an independent source of fibril-formation labels, but none of them records hexagonal-lattice geometry, so they validate a different label.

honest_claim_h3: With 13 peptides, the only honest claim a model could make is 'this reproduces the five single-residue design rules the authors already stated in the paper' - i.e. it would restate the paper's conclusions, not test them.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short peptide's amino-acid sequence to predict whether it self-assembles into a honeycomb lattice with open nanochannels.
plain_idea.train_on: The amino-acid sequence of each nine-residue peptide. Verified count: 13 peptides total (DILT1-DILT5 plus perturbations P1-P8), transcribed by hand from the paper's text.
plain_idea.predict: A yes/no call on whether the peptide forms the hexagonal, approximately 5-nm-channel lattice. The true answer comes from cryo-electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy images - specifically the presence or absence of a diagnostic striped pattern in the micrographs - scored by eye by the authors.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups designing peptide nanomaterials (filtration membranes, templated catalysis, hydrogels) would love a sequence rule for making open channels rather than solid fibrils, because every candidate currently costs a synthesis plus a cryo-electron microscopy session. But this paper supplies 13 examples, which is a hypothesis, not a training set.

more_or_better_data.why: 13 hand-transcribed peptides against published peptide self-assembly models trained on 62,000+ simulated sequences and on curated experimental amyloid databases. The one thing this data has that they lack - hexagonal channel geometry - exists for only five positive examples.

confidence_score.why: No replicate measurements, no per-peptide uncertainty, and no quantitative score at all - the readout is a by-eye yes/no on whether micrographs show stripes. Nothing here supports calibration.

models_beatable.why: AggBERT (a fine-tuned protein language model) and the Cross-Beta DB Extra Trees classifier are recent and report F1 around 0.85 on experimental amyloid labels. More importantly they solve a neighbouring task, and 13 rows cannot beat anything on any task.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: the existing models predict fibril formation, not lattice geometry, so they are not a baseline for this label; there is no shared split; and there is no accessible new data measuring hexagonal-channel formation to join on.

ml_idea: The idea considered and rejected: fine-tune or freeze a protein language model (ESM-2) on nine-residue peptide sequences to classify hexagonal-nanochannel lattice formation versus ordinary fibril formation, using the paper's DILT1-5 as positives and P1-P8 as negatives. The label is never a downloadable column, and 13 examples is far below any usable floor; the deposited assets are four atomic models and four density maps, which are a structural result, not a dataset.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed, and the numbers are meaningless in a good way: 13 nine-residue peptides embed in seconds on a laptop CPU and the whole 'dataset' is a 13-line text file I could type by hand in two hours. Cross-validation is left null because 13 rows cannot support a split.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the distinct peptide sequences in the paper. I did: 13 (five DILT variants plus eight P perturbations). That one count kills it in five minutes.

verdict_reason: A beautiful structural-biology paper with no machine-learning dataset in it. Part A fails twice: A2, because the outcome - does this peptide form a hexagonal lattice? - appears nowhere as a downloadable column and would have to be hand-built from figure captions; and A5, because the study covers 13 peptides in total against a floor of roughly 400. What was deposited is four cryo-EM maps, three released atomic models (9H7U verified: 389 KB, 54 chains of KVKVSQINM) and terabyte-scale raw movies on EMPIAR, with everything else 'available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request' and the sequences under a patent application.
